prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Starting with a field theoretic approach in Minkowski space, the gravitational energy momentum tensor is derived from the Einstein equations in a straightforward manner. This allows to present them as {\it acceleration tensor} = const. $\times$ {\it total energy momentum tensor}. For flat space cosmology the gravitational energy is negative and cancels the material energy. In the relativistic theory of gravitation a bimetric coupling between the Riemann and Minkowski metrics breaks general coordinate invariance. The case of a positive cosmological constant is considered. A singularity free version of the Schwarzschild black hole is solved analytically. In the interior the components of the metric tensor quickly die out, but do not change sign, leaving the role of time as usual. For cosmology the $\Lambda$CDM model is covered, while there appears a form of inflation at early times. Here both the total energy and the zero point energy vanish.

A field-theoretic formulation of gravity in Minkowski spacetime offers a way to define gravitational energy and momentum directly from the Einstein equations. In this framework, the equations are rearranged so that spacetime curvature—or, more specifically, an appropriate acceleration tensor—is proportional to the total energy-momentum tensor. This total tensor includes both material sources and the gravitational field itself, thereby providing a unified description of energy and momentum within a flat-background formalism.

When applied to cosmology, the approach leads to a global energy-balance condition. The gravitational field carries negative energy, which exactly compensates for the positive energy associated with matter and radiation. Consequently, the total energy of the universe vanishes. The same cancellation mechanism can also be applied to vacuum or zero-point contributions, offering an alternative perspective on the cosmological-constant and vacuum-energy problems.

The formulation employs a bimetric structure involving both a dynamical Riemannian metric and a background Minkowski metric. Coupling these two metrics selects a preferred flat-space reference structure and therefore breaks full general coordinate invariance. This modification makes it possible to analyze gravitational systems in the presence of a positive cosmological constant while retaining a field-theoretic interpretation of gravity and a well-defined energy-momentum tensor.

Within this framework, one can obtain an analytic Schwarzschild-type black-hole solution that is claimed to remain regular and free of a central singularity. The same theory also yields a cosmological model that reproduces the principal features of the standard ΛCDM scenario at late times while accommodating an inflationary phase in the early universe. Taken together, these results describe a unified gravitational framework in which black holes and cosmic evolution can be treated without singularities, while the total energy—including gravitational, material, and zero-point contributions—vanishes.

A field-theoretic formulation of gravitation in Minkowski space can be developed by rewriting Einstein’s equations so that the gravitational field is treated in a manner analogous to other relativistic fields. In this approach, the equations are used to define a gravitational energy-momentum tensor, allowing both matter and gravitation to be represented within a common energy-momentum balance. Gravity is then characterized by an acceleration tensor whose source is the total energy-momentum tensor, including contributions from matter, radiation, vacuum energy, and the gravitational field itself.

The construction employs a bimetric description. A fixed Minkowski metric provides the background spacetime and the associated global conservation laws, while an effective curved metric determines the motion of matter and the observable gravitational phenomena conventionally described by general relativity. The two metrics are coupled so that the theory reproduces relativistic gravitation while retaining an explicit local description of gravitational energy. A positive cosmological constant may be included as part of the total source.

Within this framework, the energy density assigned to the gravitational field is negative. For a spatially flat homogeneous and isotropic universe, this negative contribution can exactly compensate the positive energy associated with matter, radiation, and the cosmological term. The net energy of the universe therefore vanishes, not because its individual components are absent, but because their positive and negative contributions cancel. This result is interpreted as a direct consequence of the field equations and of total energy-momentum conservation on the Minkowski background.

The same formalism can be applied to static, spherically symmetric systems. It leads to an analytic black-hole solution related to the Schwarzschild geometry but formulated so that the time coordinate retains its timelike character throughout the physical domain. The resulting configuration is described as nonsingular in the relevant field variables and avoids the conventional interchange of temporal and radial signatures at the Schwarzschild horizon. From the bimetric perspective, the apparent horizon behavior is attributed to the effective gravitational metric rather than to a breakdown of the underlying Minkowski spacetime.

Cosmologically, the theory admits solutions that reproduce the principal features of the standard ΛCDM model, including radiation-, matter-, and cosmological-constant-dominated eras. It can also accommodate an early period of accelerated expansion corresponding to inflation. Because the gravitational contribution is included explicitly in the energy accounting, the positive energies of matter and vacuum—including zero-point energy—are balanced by negative gravitational energy. Consequently, both the total energy and the net zero-point energy vanish in the homogeneous flat cosmological solution.

Taken together, these results present gravity as a relativistic field on a flat background while preserving the effective curved-spacetime description needed for observable phenomena. The approach provides a unified energy-momentum formulation, a proposed nonsingular black-hole solution, and a cosmological model containing both ΛCDM evolution and primordial inflation. Its central claim is that a consistent inclusion of gravitational energy yields an exactly vanishing total energy for the universe.
outputs.L5:
### From Minkowski to Einstein

Starting with Hermann Minkowski’s concept of four-dimensional spacetime, modern physics gained a new way to describe the universe. Minkowski showed that space and time are not separate entities but parts of a unified structure. His mathematical framework offered a geometric interpretation of Albert Einstein’s special theory of relativity.

Einstein initially viewed Minkowski’s approach as unnecessarily abstract. However, he later recognized its importance, especially while developing general relativity. In Einstein’s theory, gravity is no longer treated as a conventional force. Instead, mass and energy curve spacetime, and objects move along paths determined by that curvature.

Thus, starting from Minkowski’s geometry, Einstein transformed our understanding of space, time, gravity, and the universe itself.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a theoretical physics paper on gravitational energy in Minkowski space, bimetric relativistic gravitation, nonsingular Schwarzschild black holes, and flat-space cosmology with a positive cosmological constant.
counterfactuals.output: We develop a bimetric formulation of relativistic gravitation in which a dynamical spacetime metric is defined over a fixed Minkowski background, allowing gravitational energy–momentum to be represented by a covariantly conserved tensor with respect to the background geometry. The field equations are examined in the static, spherically symmetric sector and shown to admit Schwarzschild-like solutions that reproduce the standard weak-field and large-radius limits while avoiding a curvature singularity through a regular interior geometry. We analyze the resulting horizon structure, causal properties, and total gravitational energy. The same framework is applied to homogeneous and isotropic cosmology with a positive cosmological constant. Although the background spacetime remains flat, the effective physical metric exhibits accelerated expansion and approaches de Sitter behavior at late times. These results illustrate how a nondynamical Minkowski structure can provide an unambiguous global notion of gravitational energy while supporting phenomenologically familiar black-hole and cosmological solutions. We also discuss the relation of the construction to general relativity, the role of the second metric, and the consistency conditions required for conservation laws and observational viability.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a field-theoretic approach to gravity in which Einstein’s equations are written as “acceleration tensor = constant × total energy-momentum tensor,” gravitational energy cancels matter energy, and general covariance is broken by coupling Riemann and Minkowski metrics.
counterfactuals.output:
This approach treats gravity as a tensor field \(h_{\mu\nu}\) propagating on a fixed Minkowski background \(\eta_{\mu\nu}\), while matter moves according to an effective curved metric
\[
g_{\mu\nu}=\eta_{\mu\nu}+h_{\mu\nu}
\]
(or a nonlinear equivalent). Einstein’s equations are rearranged into a force-field form,
\[
A_{\mu\nu}=\kappa\!\left(T^{\text{matter}}_{\mu\nu}+t^{\text{grav}}_{\mu\nu}\right),
\qquad \kappa=\frac{8\pi G}{c^{4}},
\]
where \(A_{\mu\nu}\) is interpreted as a gravitational “acceleration tensor” and \(t^{\text{grav}}_{\mu\nu}\) as the field’s own energy-momentum. The fixed background permits an ordinary conservation law for the combined matter-plus-gravity source.

In this interpretation, gravitational binding energy is negative. For a closed or suitably isolated system, it may be claimed to cancel the positive matter energy,
\[
E_{\text{matter}}+E_{\text{gravity}}=0,
\]
yielding a zero-total-energy picture of the universe.

The framework is effectively bimetric: the Riemannian metric \(g_{\mu\nu}\) governs physical rods, clocks, and free fall, while \(\eta_{\mu\nu}\) defines the background, conservation laws, and gravitational energy. Because the two metrics are coupled, the Minkowski metric introduces preferred background structure. Thus the full gauge freedom or background independence of general relativity is reduced—often described as breaking general covariance, though one can retain merely formal coordinate covariance by transforming both metrics together. The benefit is a localized gravitational energy tensor and a field-theory interpretation; the cost is dependence on an extra, potentially unobservable background geometry and possible tension with the equivalence principle.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output: We present a framework in which gravitational energy is negative in a spatially flat cosmology and balances the positive energy of matter and radiation. Within this formulation, we derive an analytic, singularity-free extension of the Schwarzschild geometry that remains regular at both the event horizon and the origin. The construction preserves the physical time coordinate across the horizon, avoiding the conventional interchange of temporal and radial roles in the black-hole interior. Applied cosmologically, the model reproduces the principal background behavior associated with \(\Lambda\)CDM while providing a geometric interpretation of accelerated expansion. At high curvature, the same regularization mechanism generates an early inflationary phase without an initial singularity. These results suggest a unified description of black-hole interiors, gravitational energy, late-time acceleration, and primordial inflation, and motivate further tests of the model’s stability and observational predictions.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how a bimetric theory of gravitation with a Minkowski background can address gravitational energy, a positive cosmological constant, black-hole singularities, zero-point energy, and the vanishing total energy of the universe.
counterfactuals.output:
A bimetric theory supplements the physical spacetime metric \(g_{\mu\nu}\), which governs clocks and matter, with a flat reference metric \(\eta_{\mu\nu}\). A schematic action is

\[
S=\frac{M_{\rm Pl}^{2}}{2}\int d^4x\,\sqrt{-g}
\left[R(g)-2\Lambda-m^2V(g^{-1}\eta)\right]+S_{\rm matter}[g,\psi].
\]

The fixed Minkowski metric gives a preferred background against which gravitational fields, energies, and boundary conditions can be defined. Depending on the interaction potential \(V\), this framework can address the listed issues as follows.

### 1. Gravitational energy

In general relativity, gravitational energy is usually represented by coordinate-dependent pseudotensors because there is no fixed spacetime geometry with respect to which translations are defined. A Minkowski background supplies global translation symmetries and an unambiguous volume element. One can therefore define a gravitational stress-energy tensor by varying the gravitational action with respect to the background metric:

\[
t_{\rm grav}^{\mu\nu}
\equiv -\frac{2}{\sqrt{-\eta}}
\frac{\delta S_{\rm grav}}{\delta \eta_{\mu\nu}}.
\]

The field equations then imply a background conservation law of the form

\[
\partial_\mu\!\left(T_{\rm matter}^{\mu\nu}
+t_{\rm grav}^{\mu\nu}\right)=0.
\]

Thus gravitational energy can be treated as a genuine background tensor rather than merely as a coordinate-dependent pseudotensor. Its localization is nevertheless theory-dependent and may still be altered by improvement terms.

### 2. A positive cosmological constant

The interaction between the two metrics acts like an effective stress tensor. For suitable parameters, it admits solutions in which \(g_{\mu\nu}\) is de Sitter-like even though the reference metric remains Minkowski:

\[
G_{\mu\nu}(g)+m^2 X_{\mu\nu}(g,\eta)
+\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}=8\pi G T_{\mu\nu}.
\]

On a cosmological branch, \(X_{\mu\nu}\) can be proportional to \(g_{\mu\nu}\), giving

\[
\Lambda_{\rm eff}=\Lambda+\Lambda_{\rm interaction}>0.
\]

Cosmic acceleration can therefore arise from a bare cosmological constant, from the metric-interaction potential, or from both. In massive-gravity language this is associated with the graviton mass and its nonlinear potential.

### 3. Black-hole singularities

The second metric or mass term modifies gravity when the physical metric becomes extremely strong relative to the background. In some models, the equations prevent the physical lapse from reaching zero, impose a causality condition between the two light cones, or generate an effective repulsive pressure near the would-be horizon. Collapse may then produce a very compact horizonless object, a bounce, or a nonsingular core instead of the Schwarzschild singularity.

The background also makes it meaningful to distinguish a degeneracy of \(g_{\mu\nu}\) from a pathology of the underlying manifold. However, singularity avoidance is not automatic: many massive and bimetric theories possess ordinary black-hole solutions, curvature singularities, unstable branches, or strong-coupling problems. It depends critically on the chosen interaction potential and matter dynamics.

### 4. Zero-point energy

Because Minkowski space is a distinguished vacuum, one can define energy relative to that vacuum and subtract the state-independent zero-point contribution:

\[
\langle T_{\mu\nu}\rangle_{\rm ren}
=
\langle T_{\mu\nu}\rangle-
\langle 0_{\eta}|T_{\mu\nu}|0_{\eta}\rangle.
\]

Some formulations also arrange for a constant vacuum-energy term to be absorbed into the metric-interaction potential or canceled by the gravitational background contribution. In that sense, only energy differences or departures from the reference vacuum gravitate.

This does **not by itself solve the cosmological-constant problem**. Quantum corrections generally renormalize every allowed constant term in the action, so a symmetry or dynamical cancellation mechanism is still needed to explain why the observed \(\Lambda_{\rm eff}\) is so small.

### 5. Vanishing total energy of the universe

The background conservation law allows a total four-momentum to be defined on a Minkowski-time hypersurface:

\[
P^\nu=\int_\Sigma d^3x\,
\left(T_{\rm matter}^{0\nu}+t_{\rm grav}^{0\nu}\right).
\]

For a closed universe, or for boundary conditions with no net flux at infinity, this quantity is conserved. Certain cosmological solutions have

\[
E_{\rm matter}+E_{\rm grav}+E_{\rm vacuum}=0,
\]

because positive matter and vacuum energy are balanced by negative gravitational binding energy. The universe can then evolve without acquiring a nonzero net Noether energy relative to the background.

Again, zero total energy is a property of particular solutions and boundary conditions, not a universal theorem of every bimetric model. It is best understood as a precise realization of the heuristic statement that the positive energy of matter can be canceled by the negative energy stored in the gravitational field.

Overall, the Minkowski background provides the bookkeeping structure needed to define gravitational energy and vacuum subtraction, while the metric-interaction terms can mimic a positive cosmological constant and alter strong-field collapse. Whether all these benefits occur consistently requires a ghost-free, stable interaction and appropriate solutions; they are possibilities of bimetric gravity rather than generic guarantees.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a technical overview of a relativistic gravity model that derives a gravitational energy-momentum tensor from Einstein’s equations, breaks general coordinate invariance through bimetric coupling, and yields both nonsingular black holes and a flat cosmology compatible with $\Lambda$CDM.
counterfactuals.output:
## Bimetric gravitational–energy–momentum model

The model can be formulated as a background-dependent, bimetric extension of general relativity in which gravity possesses a genuine local energy–momentum tensor. It is closely related to field-theoretic or Logunov-type relativistic theories of gravitation.

### 1. Two-metric structure

The theory contains

- a **dynamical metric** \(g_{\mu\nu}\), which determines proper times, matter propagation, and curvature;
- a fixed or nondynamical **reference metric** \(f_{\mu\nu}\), usually Minkowski,
  \[
  R_{\mu\nu}[f]=0.
  \]

The action has the schematic form

\[
S=
\frac{M_{\rm Pl}^{2}}{2}
\int d^{4}x\,\sqrt{-g}
\left[
R(g)-2\Lambda-m^{2}U(g^{-1}f)
\right]
+S_{\rm m}[g,\psi].
\]

Here \(U(g^{-1}f)\) is a nonderivative interaction between the two metrics. It may represent a graviton-mass term, a preferred-frame coupling, or a more general bimetric potential.

If \(f_{\mu\nu}\) is fixed, only transformations acting simultaneously on \(g_{\mu\nu}\) and \(f_{\mu\nu}\) remain as formal covariance. Active transformations of \(g_{\mu\nu}\) relative to the fixed background are no longer gauge redundancies. Thus the unrestricted general-coordinate invariance of general relativity is physically broken or reduced.

### 2. Gravitational energy–momentum tensor

Einstein’s equations may be written as

\[
G_{\mu\nu}(g)+\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}
=
8\pi G\,T_{\mu\nu}^{\rm m}
+m^{2}X_{\mu\nu}(g,f),
\]

where

\[
X_{\mu\nu}
=
-\frac{2}{\sqrt{-g}}
\frac{\delta}{\delta g^{\mu\nu}}
\left(\sqrt{-g}\,U\right).
\]

The background metric makes it possible to define a true gravitational stress tensor by variation with respect to \(f_{\mu\nu}\):

\[
t_{\rm grav}^{\mu\nu}
\equiv
-\frac{2}{\sqrt{-f}}
\frac{\delta S_{\rm grav}}{\delta f_{\mu\nu}} .
\]

Equivalently, one can rearrange the Einstein tensor into a field equation on the reference geometry,

\[
\mathcal E_f^{\mu\nu}(h)
=
8\pi G\left(
T_{\rm m}^{\mu\nu}+t_{\rm grav}^{\mu\nu}
\right),
\qquad
h_{\mu\nu}=g_{\mu\nu}-f_{\mu\nu},
\]

where \(\mathcal E_f^{\mu\nu}\) is the part linear in the gravitational field and the nonlinear remainder defines \(t_{\rm grav}^{\mu\nu}\).

Unlike the familiar Einstein, Landau–Lifshitz, or Møller pseudotensors, \(t_{\rm grav}^{\mu\nu}\) is a tensor under the residual coordinate group because the reference geometry supplies an invariant standard for separating inertial structure from gravity. It obeys a background-covariant conservation law,

\[
D_\mu^{(f)}
\left(
T_{\rm m}^{\mu\nu}+t_{\rm grav}^{\mu\nu}
\right)=0.
\]

The price is that gravitational energy is no longer defined independently of the chosen background.

### 3. Constraint sector

The Bianchi identity,

\[
\nabla_\mu^{(g)}G^{\mu\nu}=0,
\]

combined with matter conservation implies

\[
\nabla_\mu^{(g)}X^{\mu\nu}=0.
\]

In massive or fixed-background formulations this becomes a physical constraint rather than a freely chosen coordinate condition. A common version is

\[
D_\mu^{(f)}
\left(\sqrt{-g}\,g^{\mu\nu}\right)=0.
\]

These four conditions remove otherwise redundant components of \(g_{\mu\nu}\), select the preferred relation between the two metrics, and play an important role in both spherical and cosmological solutions.

### 4. Nonsingular compact objects

For a static, spherically symmetric geometry,

\[
ds_g^{2}
=
-A(r)\,dt^{2}
+B(r)\,dr^{2}
+r^{2}d\Omega^{2},
\]

the bimetric contribution acts as an effective source,

\[
T_{\mu\nu}^{\rm eff}
=
T_{\mu\nu}^{\rm m}
+\frac{m^{2}}{8\pi G}X_{\mu\nu}.
\]

At large radius one recovers Schwarzschild behavior,

\[
A(r)\simeq 1-\frac{2GM}{r},
\qquad
B(r)\simeq
\left(1-\frac{2GM}{r}\right)^{-1},
\]

up to Yukawa or cosmological corrections. Near the nominal Schwarzschild radius, however, the potential \(U(g^{-1}f)\) becomes important. It can prevent \(A(r)\) from reaching zero or replace the Schwarzschild interior by a regular de Sitter-like core,

\[
A(r)\simeq 1-\frac{r^{2}}{r_{0}^{2}},
\qquad
R,\;R_{\mu\nu}R^{\mu\nu},\;
R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}R^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}<\infty .
\]

Depending on the chosen potential and parameters, the result is either

1. a **regular black hole**, with horizons but no curvature singularity, or  
2. a highly redshifted, horizonless “black-star” or “frozen-star” configuration.

Thus “nonsingular black hole” should not automatically be interpreted as an exact Schwarzschild black hole: some versions remove the singularity while retaining horizons, whereas Logunov-type versions often prevent the formation of a true event horizon.

### 5. Homogeneous cosmology

For a spatially flat ansatz,

\[
ds_g^{2}
=
-N^{2}(t)dt^{2}
+a^{2}(t)d\mathbf x^{2},
\]

the modified Friedmann equations can be written as

\[
3H^{2}
=
8\pi G
\left(
\rho_{\rm m}+\rho_{\rm r}+\rho_{\rm grav}
\right)
+\Lambda,
\]

\[
-2\dot H-3H^{2}
=
8\pi G
\left(
p_{\rm r}+p_{\rm grav}
\right)-\Lambda,
\]

with

\[
\rho_{\rm grav}
=
-\frac{m^{2}M_{\rm Pl}^{2}}{2}X^{0}{}_{0},
\qquad
p_{\rm grav}
=
\frac{m^{2}M_{\rm Pl}^{2}}{6}X^{i}{}_{i}.
\]

The constraint equation fixes the lapse or the ratio between the physical and reference scale factors. In many realizations it also selects \(k=0\), making spatial flatness structural rather than an inflationary initial-condition problem.

The interaction sector generally decomposes into terms with different scale-factor dependence,

\[
\rho_{\rm grav}(a)
=
\rho_{\Lambda}^{\rm eff}
+\rho_{1}a^{-1}
+\rho_{2}a^{-2}
+\rho_{3}a^{-3}
+\rho_{4}a^{-4}
+\cdots .
\]

Parameters can be chosen so that the nonconstant terms are negligible after nucleosynthesis, leaving

\[
H^{2}(a)\simeq
H_{0}^{2}
\left[
\Omega_{\rm r}a^{-4}
+\Omega_{\rm m}a^{-3}
+\Omega_{\Lambda}
\right],
\qquad
\Omega_{\rm r}+\Omega_{\rm m}+\Omega_\Lambda=1.
\]

The background expansion is then observationally indistinguishable, or nearly so, from flat \(\Lambda\)CDM. At very small \(a\), additional terms can cause

\[
H^{2}(a_{\min})=0,
\qquad a_{\min}>0,
\]

producing a bounce and eliminating the big-bang curvature singularity.

### 6. Interpretation and consistency issues

The model’s central trade-off is:

- **Gain:** a local gravitational energy–momentum tensor, an unambiguous background conservation law, and modified strong-field/cosmological behavior.
- **Cost:** preferred background structure and loss of full diffeomorphism gauge symmetry.

Its viability depends on the detailed bimetric potential. A generic potential can propagate an unwanted scalar—the Boulware–Deser ghost—or produce gradient instabilities, negative-energy modes, or conflict with gravitational-wave bounds. A complete model must therefore demonstrate:

\[
\text{no ghosts},\qquad
\text{no tachyonic/gradient instabilities},\qquad
c_{\rm GW}\simeq c,
\]

together with recovery of general relativity in the Solar System, usually through a small graviton mass or a nonlinear screening mechanism.

In summary, the construction treats gravity as a tensor field relative to a reference geometry. That reference metric converts the nonlinear part of Einstein’s equations into a genuine gravitational energy–momentum tensor, while the associated bimetric interaction modifies the near-horizon and early-universe regimes. Suitable choices yield regular compact objects, a nonsingular or bouncing cosmology, enforced spatial flatness, and a late-time expansion matching flat \(\Lambda\)CDM.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
